project.name: byop
project.description: Bring Your Own Provider (BYOP) is an interactive CLI that wires a custom OpenAI-compatible LLM provider into Zed, py.dev, and other AI coding tools.

nodes.name: __init__.py
nodes.summary: Defines the package public API by re-exporting provider models and legacy apply helpers, and resolves the installed BYOP version with a development fallback.

nodes.name: __init__.py
nodes.summary: Collects the core configuration, orchestration, prompting, key storage, settings, and Zed helpers into a stable package-level API.

nodes.name: apply.py
nodes.summary: Provides compatibility orchestration that delegates provider fragment generation, configuration, and provider discovery to the Zed target abstraction.

nodes.name: default_model_capabilities
nodes.summary: Returns the baseline capability flags used for OpenAI-compatible chat models.

nodes.name: build_settings_update
nodes.summary: Delegates to ZedTarget to build the complete settings fragment for a provider.

nodes.name: apply_provider
nodes.summary: Configures Zed through the target abstraction with dry-run and secret-storage choices, then returns the generated fragment.

nodes.name: current_provider_names
nodes.summary: Reads configured OpenAI-compatible provider names through a path-specific Zed target.

nodes.name: keychain.py
nodes.summary: Stores OpenAI-compatible provider secrets in the macOS login keychain or shell profiles, with explicit handling for missing entries and secure command references.
nodes.languageNotes: Shell-bound values are quoted before being embedded in Zed command references, while subprocess exit code 44 is treated as the keychain not-found sentinel.

nodes.name: _run
nodes.summary: Executes a command without raising so callers can interpret security-tool exit codes explicitly.

nodes.name: keychain_has
nodes.summary: Checks for a matching internet-password item, mapping only the not-found exit code to false and surfacing other failures.

nodes.name: security_command_ref
nodes.summary: Builds a shell-quoted Zed command reference that retrieves a keychain secret at request time.

nodes.name: keychain_get
nodes.summary: Returns a stored keychain secret, distinguishes a missing item from operational errors, and strips command output.

nodes.name: keychain_set
nodes.summary: Replaces a provider secret by deleting any prior entry and adding a new login-keychain internet password.

nodes.name: keychain_delete
nodes.summary: Deletes a provider keychain entry while treating absence as benign and propagating unexpected security errors.

nodes.name: env_var_export_line
nodes.summary: Formats a shell export statement for a provider API key.

nodes.name: profile_candidates
nodes.summary: Returns the ordered shell profile paths searched for existing provider exports.

nodes.name: find_env_in_profiles
nodes.summary: Finds the first readable shell profile that already exports the requested environment variable.

nodes.name: write_env_to_profile
nodes.summary: Appends a provider key export to a selected shell profile without duplicating an identical existing line.

nodes.name: ensure_key
nodes.summary: Coordinates keychain and environment-profile storage, logs each selected action, and rejects an empty storage policy.

nodes.name: settings.py
nodes.summary: Parses JSONC settings without damaging comment-like string content, recursively merges updates, and serializes settings to disk.
nodes.languageNotes: A small string-state scanner removes JSONC comments while preserving URLs, escapes, and other comment-like content inside quoted strings.

nodes.name: _strip_comments
nodes.summary: Scans JSONC text character by character to remove line and block comments only when outside quoted strings.

nodes.name: loads
nodes.summary: Normalizes JSONC comments and trailing commas before parsing the result as JSON.

nodes.name: load_path
nodes.summary: Loads a JSONC settings file or returns an empty mapping when the path does not exist.

nodes.name: merge
nodes.summary: Recursively combines nested mappings into a new dictionary while replacing scalar or incompatible values.

nodes.name: dumps
nodes.summary: Serializes settings as readable Unicode JSON with a trailing newline.

nodes.name: write_path
nodes.summary: Creates missing parent directories and writes serialized settings to the requested path.

nodes.name: zed.py
nodes.summary: Detects, installs, upgrades, and reports Zed on macOS using Homebrew when available and GitHub release downloads as a fallback.
nodes.languageNotes: A dataclass carries installation status, while platform and networking modules are imported lazily on the direct-download path.

nodes.name: _run
nodes.summary: Runs a platform command with optional output capture and leaves return-code handling to the caller.

nodes.name: _bundle_version
nodes.summary: Reads the installed Zed bundle version from its macOS property list when the application exists.

nodes.name: has_brew
nodes.summary: Reports whether the Homebrew executable is available on PATH.

nodes.name: is_installed
nodes.summary: Reports whether the Zed application bundle exists in Applications.

nodes.name: installed_version
nodes.summary: Returns the installed Zed bundle version when it can be resolved.

nodes.name: brew_installed
nodes.summary: Uses Homebrew cask metadata to determine whether Homebrew manages the Zed installation.

nodes.name: status
nodes.summary: Combines application presence, bundle version, and Homebrew ownership into a ZedStatus value.

nodes.name: install
nodes.summary: Installs or upgrades Zed through Homebrew when possible and otherwise selects the direct-download path.

nodes.name: upgrade
nodes.summary: Upgrades a Homebrew-managed Zed installation, tolerates the already-current result, or reinstalls a direct download.

nodes.name: _install_via_download
nodes.summary: Downloads the architecture-specific Zed disk image, mounts and copies the application, detaches it, and links the CLI.

nodes.name: latest_release_tag
nodes.summary: Fetches the latest GitHub release metadata and returns its tag name.

nodes.name: json_loads
nodes.summary: Parses a JSON string using the standard library.

nodes.name: ZedStatus
nodes.summary: Carries whether Zed is installed, its detected version, and whether Homebrew manages it.

nodes.name: __init__.py
nodes.summary: Defines the target package API, eagerly exposing the shared protocol and registry while lazily loading platform-specific target classes on first access.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses Python module-level __getattr__ (PEP 562) to provide lazy re-exports without importing macOS-specific modules on unsupported platforms.

nodes.name: __getattr__
nodes.summary: Lazily imports and returns requested target classes while rejecting unknown package attributes.

nodes.name: base.py
nodes.summary: Defines the structural Target protocol and shared helpers for detecting installed applications and applying one provider configuration across multiple targets.
nodes.languageNotes: A runtime-checkable Protocol keeps target implementations duck-typed while allowing runtime conformance checks.

nodes.name: detect_installed
nodes.summary: Filters a target list to instances whose installation probe succeeds.

nodes.name: configure_all
nodes.summary: Configures each target sequentially with one provider while forwarding dry-run, credential, and logging options.

nodes.name: Target
nodes.summary: Specifies the runtime-checkable interface required of every configurable application target.

nodes.name: omp.py
nodes.summary: Adapts the py.dev provider model to Oh My Pi, resolving profile-specific models.yml paths, round-tripping a constrained YAML schema without PyYAML, and installing OMP through supported package channels.
nodes.languageNotes: Implements a deliberately constrained recursive YAML parser and emitter with only the scalar, mapping, sequence, and flow-list forms generated by BYOP.

nodes.name: profile_models_path
nodes.summary: Validates an OMP profile name and resolves its isolated models.yml path beneath the selected configuration root.

nodes.name: _yaml_scalar
nodes.summary: Renders supported Python primitive values as safe single-line YAML scalars.

nodes.name: _parse_models_yaml
nodes.summary: Parses the constrained YAML mapping, sequence, flow-list, and scalar subset accepted for OMP models configuration.

nodes.name: _emit_value
nodes.summary: Recursively renders dictionaries, lists, and scalars as correctly indented YAML lines.

nodes.name: _emit_models_yaml
nodes.summary: Serializes a provider fragment into OMP's deterministic models.yml layout while retaining supported extra provider and model fields.

nodes.name: OmpTarget
nodes.summary: Extends PyTarget for OMP by switching persistence to profile-aware YAML and adding OMP-specific detection and installation.

nodes.name: opencode.py
nodes.summary: Builds and merges OpenCode provider configuration, maps model capabilities to the OpenAI-compatible SDK schema, resolves provider-name conflicts, and keeps API keys in the macOS keychain when available.

nodes.name: OpencodeTarget
nodes.summary: Implements OpenCode provider installation, fragment generation, conflict-aware JSON persistence, secure credentials, and configuration export.

nodes.name: py.py
nodes.summary: Configures py.dev models.json with OpenAI-compatible providers and model capabilities, preserving other providers while handling conflicts and secure keychain-backed API-key references.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses Pi's !command credential form to defer API-key lookup to the macOS keychain at runtime.

nodes.name: PyTarget
nodes.summary: Implements py.dev installation and conflict-aware models.json configuration with model capability mapping and keychain-backed credentials.

nodes.name: registry.py
nodes.summary: Maintains the supported target class registry and instantiates each target with optional Zed settings and OMP profile or models-path overrides.

nodes.name: available_targets
nodes.summary: Instantiates every registered target, applying optional custom paths to Zed and OMP-specific profile settings.

nodes.name: zed.py
nodes.summary: Builds and merges Zed OpenAI-compatible provider settings, manages idempotent conflict handling, stores credentials through the keychain layer, and exports only BYOP-managed configuration.

nodes.name: ZedTarget
nodes.summary: Implements Zed installation, provider-settings generation and merge, idempotent conflict handling, keychain storage, and managed-config export.

tour.title: Project Purpose and Safety
tour.description: Start with README.md to understand BYOP's purpose: turning one OpenAI-compatible provider definition into safe configurations for multiple AI coding tools. The Documentation and Product Specifications layer explains installation, profiles, conflict behavior, generated files, and the invariant that secrets are not written to plaintext configuration. This context supplies the vocabulary and safety model for every later step.

tour.title: CLI Entry and API
tour.description: With the product context established, byop.cli:main is the runtime entry point declared by the package manifest. cli.py owns parsing, legacy and subcommand routing, profile commands, diagnostics, export, and provider application, while the package initializers expose the stable public surfaces around that orchestration. This is the Command-Line Application layer's bird's-eye view before following its dependencies outward.
tour.languageLesson: Python console entry points name a module and callable, so byop = byop.cli:main lets packaging generate an executable without a separate launcher module. Package __init__.py files can then curate imports into a deliberate public API.

tour.title: Provider Input Pipeline
tour.description: Following the CLI's orchestration, the provider dataclasses establish the normalized domain model and validate OpenAI-compatible inputs. Paste parsing, terminal prompts, and the wizard turn strict JSON, JSONC, aliases, or interactive answers into that model, while the conflict module determines each target's replace-or-append policy. Together these files keep parsing, validation, and policy decisions ahead of filesystem or credential side effects.
tour.languageLesson: Python dataclasses make the provider and model records explicit, while pure validation and policy functions keep invalid states from reaching side-effecting adapters. JSONC parsing must distinguish actual comments from comment-like text inside quoted strings.

tour.title: Profiles Secrets and Settings
tour.description: Once a provider is normalized, the Provider Domain and Persistence layer decides what may persist and where. Platform-aware paths and secret-free TOML profiles preserve reusable metadata, JSONC settings merge non-destructively, and the keychain layer keeps credentials behind secure references or controlled shell-profile exports. This separation centralizes host I/O and explains the security and idempotency assumptions used by every target adapter.
tour.languageLesson: TOML preserves typed profile metadata in a human-readable form, while JSONC permits comments and trailing commas that a strict JSON parser rejects. Credentials remain outside both formats, so serialization and secret storage have separate trust boundaries.

tour.title: Target Adapter Contract
tour.description: With shared input and persistence established, the Coding Tool Adapters layer defines the seam between BYOP and each external application. The structural Target protocol, target registry, lazy target-package exports, and multi-target helpers provide common discovery and application behavior; the compatibility apply module delegates the older Zed flow through the same abstraction. This is the extension point to understand before reading any concrete tool schema.
tour.languageLesson: A Python Protocol provides structural typing: a target satisfies the contract by implementing the required members without inheriting a base class. Lazy imports keep platform-specific adapters out of startup paths until callers request them.

tour.title: Zed Integration Path
tour.description: The Zed implementation is the first concrete path through the adapter contract. The target adapter generates and idempotently merges provider settings, resolves conflicts, stores credentials through the keychain layer, and exports only BYOP-managed configuration; the legacy Zed module handles macOS detection, installation, and upgrades through Homebrew or release downloads. Keeping application lifecycle separate from configuration mutation makes this pair a useful reference for the remaining adapters.

tour.title: JSON Tool Adapters
tour.description: With the Zed pattern in mind, compare the py.dev, OpenCode, and Claude Code adapters. Each maps the shared provider and model capabilities into a different JSON schema, preserves unrelated configuration, resolves naming conflicts, and chooses a keychain-backed or literal credential form appropriate to the tool. Their differences show why common orchestration belongs in the protocol while schema and installation knowledge remain local to each adapter.

tour.title: OMP and Warp Boundaries
tour.description: The final adapter pair demonstrates two different boundaries: OMP maps the provider into profile-specific models.yml files, while Warp validates public HTTPS endpoints and emits redacted manual instructions rather than guessing an undocumented settings schema. The Warp product requirements and dependency-ordered tickets record that refusal as a release safety gate, alongside dry-run, TOML, and smoke-test expectations. Together they cap the adapter layer by contrasting supported serialization with deliberate non-automation.
tour.languageLesson: YAML is indentation-sensitive, so OMP deliberately round-trips only its constrained schema without introducing a general YAML dependency. TOML carries typed values, but syntactically valid output is still unsafe when the receiving application's schema is undocumented.

tour.title: Domain and Security Tests
tour.description: After tracing the runtime layers, enter the Test Suite at the core domain and persistence boundaries. These tests cover provider serialization and validation, profile path and TOML behavior, non-mutating JSONC merges, keychain and shell-profile failure handling, and conflict-policy precedence. By isolating filesystem and subprocess effects, they defend the invariants that all adapters share.

tour.title: CLI Interaction Tests
tour.description: Building on those core contracts, the application tests exercise the user-facing composition of the CLI, wizard, paste parser, prompt sanitizer, and legacy apply path. They cover routing, cancellation, target selection, dry-run isolation, malformed or partial input, multiple models, escape-byte handling, and mocked host mutations. This group shows how the Command-Line Application remains testable despite its interactive surface.

tour.title: Adapter Contract Tests
tour.description: The next tests verify the shared adapter contract, Zed's installation boundary, and the read-only export surface. Registry membership, installation filtering, generated fragments, merge and conflict behavior, dry runs, provider filtering, and exported snapshots are all checked without touching real applications. This validates the common topology before the remaining tool-specific edge cases.

tour.title: Target-Specific Tests
tour.description: The remaining adapter suites mirror the OMP, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Warp implementations from Steps 7 and 8. They exercise installation fallbacks, profile and file-format semantics, merge conflicts, registry integration, credential handling, and Warp's endpoint and redaction safeguards. Comparing them reveals a common Target contract without erasing each application's distinct safety rules.

tour.title: Packaging and Installation
tour.description: Once behavior is protected, the Package API and Installation layer explains how BYOP becomes an installable command. pyproject.toml defines the setuptools build, dependencies, tool configuration, package data, and byop = byop.cli:main entry point; py.typed advertises inline typing, while install.sh locates Python and pipx, resolves a release, installs the package, and checks PATH exposure. These files connect the CLI entry from Step 2 to a typed distribution that can be bootstrapped on macOS.
tour.languageLesson: In pyproject.toml, the [project.scripts] table maps a shell command to a Python module callable. An empty py.typed file is meaningful under PEP 561: packaging it tells type checkers that the installed library includes inline annotations.

tour.title: Delivery and CI
tour.description: The installable artifact then feeds the Delivery Infrastructure and CI layer. worker.js serves the landing and install endpoints, resolves the latest GitHub release, and handles caching, CORS, and failures; wrangler.toml binds that Worker to the BYOP domain, while the CI workflow runs linting, typing, and tests across supported Python versions before building distributions. These nodes connect source assurance to the download path used by the bootstrap installer.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions YAML organizes parallelizable jobs and sequential steps, with dependencies gating distribution builds on successful checks. Cloudflare's TOML deployment configuration binds the JavaScript Worker entry point to its runtime and custom domain.

tour.title: Evolution and Contributor Context
tour.description: Finish in the Documentation and Product Specifications layer by placing the current architecture in its maintenance history. AGENTS.md records contributor-facing layout, conventions, safety invariants, and development workflow; the v1.5.0 specification explains configuration export and prompt sanitization, while the v2.0.0 specification explains profiles, explicit subcommands, status, and backward compatibility. Reading these after the implementation distinguishes enduring contracts from release-specific changes and shows where future behavior should be documented.
tour.languageLesson: Markdown specifications turn architectural intent and acceptance criteria into reviewable history, complementing executable tests with the reasons behind compatibility and safety decisions.
